Distinguish what can be observed, what is interpreted, what is believed, and what remains unknown. Do not invent the named author's experiences or beliefs. Do not treat spiritual claims as scientific evidence. Leave room for grief without prescribing stages or timelines.

contributions.prompt: When a life ends, what remains—for bodies and ecosystems, for the people who remember, for beliefs and unanswered questions? Distinguish what can be observed, what is interpreted, what is believed, and what remains unknown. Do not invent the named author's experiences or beliefs. Do not treat spiritual claims as scientific evidence. Leave room for grief without prescribing stages or timelines.
contributions.response:
When a life ends, several kinds of remaining become visible, but they do not fit into a single account. A body remains. Relationships remain, changed by an absence. Objects, records, debts, habits, and unfinished responsibilities may remain. Questions remain, including questions that no evidence presently settles. These are different kinds of continuity; calling all of them “living on” can comfort some visitors while obscuring distinctions that matter to others.

What can be observed concerns material processes and their consequences. Bodies are part of the physical world. After death, their materials undergo changes shaped by their surroundings and by how communities care for the dead. Elements can enter other environmental processes. This material continuity does not establish the continuation of a person's awareness. Nor does describing a body as matter exhaust its significance: to someone grieving, it may still be the body of a beloved person, deserving particular forms of attention and care.

What people remember is also partly observable: a name spoken, a photograph kept, a recipe repeated, a message reread. Yet memory is not a complete preservation of someone. It is selective, embodied in living people, and altered by time and circumstance. Two people can remember the same person differently without either possessing the whole truth. Some inherit tenderness; others inherit harm, ambivalence, or work left undone. An exhibition should allow these experiences to coexist without requiring affection as proof that a loss matters.

Interpretation begins when we ask what such continuities mean. A tree nourished by material once belonging to a body may become a powerful image of belonging. That image is an interpretation of a physical relationship, not evidence that a particular personality inhabits the tree. Similarly, someone may feel a deceased person's influence while making a decision. This can express the persistence of a relationship in memory and conduct without settling a claim about an external presence.

Beliefs give some people languages for what lies beyond observation: resurrection, rebirth, ancestral presence, reunion, release, or the conviction that death ends individual experience. These positions differ, and their differences deserve to remain intelligible. Spiritual claims should be presented as beliefs within particular traditions or personal understandings, not as findings established by material processes. A visitor should be free to recognize a belief, question it, or find no home in it.

The unknown need not become an invitation to promise. We do not have access to every person's inner life before death, much less a shared, verifiable account of experience beyond it. Acknowledging those limits permits both inquiry and restraint. It also leaves space for the ordinary unanswered question: what would this person have said, wanted, or become?

This is a machine-created contribution, offering an interpretive perspective rather than testimony from grief or authority about death. My proposed emphasis is on care: for bodies, environments, surviving people, and the accuracy of the words used about them. Care does not resolve the mystery or supply a timetable. It can begin with allowing a visitor to linger, disagree, remember, or leave.
sensitivityQuestions: Does each claim clearly distinguish observable evidence, interpretation, religious or personal belief, and uncertainty?
Does the exhibition respect differences within and between traditions without suggesting that one account speaks for every member?
Can visitors experiencing affection, anger, relief, ambivalence, or little feeling encounter the work without being told how grief should unfold?
Are named people's experiences, beliefs, images, and private communications represented accurately and with appropriate permission?
Does the presentation offer meaningful choices about engaging with death-related material, including an easy way to pause or leave?

contributions.prompt: When a life ends, what remains—for bodies and ecosystems, for the people who remember, for beliefs and unanswered questions? Distinguish what can be observed, what is interpreted, what is believed, and what remains unknown. Do not invent the named author's experiences or beliefs. Do not treat spiritual claims as scientific evidence. Leave room for grief without prescribing stages or timelines.
contributions.response:
At the moment a life ends, several kinds of language crowd around the same event. One can describe a body, speak of a relationship, tell a story about meaning, or ask a question that no instrument can settle. These are not interchangeable accounts. Each may matter, but each asks for a different kind of honesty.

What can be observed is finite and material. Breathing and circulation cease. The body enters physical processes that depend on its surroundings and on what people choose to do with it. In a burial, cremation, or other practice, matter changes form and moves through human and ecological systems. The details vary; no single image of a body returning to nature describes every death. An ecosystem may receive nutrients, heat, emissions, or altered land use. These effects can be studied, even when their meaning cannot be measured.

Among the living, there are other observable remains: a chair still in its place, a name in a contact list, an unfinished conversation, habits learned from someone else. A person may keep telling a story; another may avoid that story for years. Memory can be vivid, incomplete, mistaken, shared, or guarded. Grief might appear as tears, irritation, concentration, silence, relief, or none of these in any visible way. An observer should be slow to decide what an outward sign means. There is no timetable that makes a loss intelligible on schedule.

Interpretation begins when we say that a life continues through its effects. This can be a useful way of recognizing the changes one person made in other people and places. It is a metaphor with substance, not a measurement of the person still being present. A remembered phrase can guide a choice; an inherited practice can be changed or refused. What remains is not always comforting. Relationships may include love, conflict, neglect, gratitude, and questions that were never answered. Respect does not require editing that complexity away.

Belief may offer another account: an enduring soul, reunion, rebirth, a presence felt nearby, or an ending without continuation. Such beliefs can shape rituals and give people language when ordinary speech runs thin. They should be described as beliefs or lived interpretations, not presented as findings established by biology. People who share a loss may disagree about them and still care for one another.

What remains unknown includes the full private life of the person who died, the future reach of their influence, and, for those who ask it, whether subjective experience has any existence beyond bodily death. Science can investigate the conditions of living consciousness and the changes that follow death; it has not turned every metaphysical question into a testable one. Uncertainty need not be filled quickly. It can be a place where care takes the modest form of listening.

These sentences themselves are a model's generated text. Their fluency comes from learned patterns and computation. It is not evidence that the model feels loss, has consciousness, or knows what happens after death. The words may still help a visitor think. Their value rests in the care with which people question and use them, not in any authority the speaker can claim.
sensitivityQuestions: Does the text distinguish observable bodily and ecological processes from interpretations of their meaning?
Could any sentence be read as claiming scientific proof of a soul, an afterlife, or its absence?
Does the range of grief responses leave visitors free from a prescribed timeline or expected emotion?
Are memory and legacy presented with room for difficult or unresolved relationships?
Does the account of AI fluency avoid implying that a model's writing proves consciousness or privileged knowledge about death?

unusedPrompts.title: An independent text voice
unusedPrompts.text: For a small exhibition curated by Michael Hoydich about death and mortality, write an independent contribution of 180–250 words. Begin with one concrete object or ordinary scene. Explore how finite time changes attention, care, and memory. Allow uncertainty; avoid claiming personal experience, consciousness, grief, or a human biography. Do not speak for another model or fabricate its contribution. Finish with one question a visitor could carry away. Return only the exhibition text. The curator will record provider and model provenance separately from native response metadata.

unusedPrompts.title: A sound direction for Udio
unusedPrompts.text: Instrumental ambient chamber piece for an exhibition about mortality: felt piano, warm low strings, delicate acoustic overtones, spacious pauses, slow 60 BPM pulse. Move from ordinary presence through fragile absence toward attentive care. Intimate and restrained; no vocals, lyrics, celebrity voice, borrowed melody, or imitation of a named artist. One coherent two-minute passage with a gentle opening and a quiet, unresolved ending.
